title: Argentine couple to return Nazi-looted painting to rightful owner
description: A painting which was stolen by the Nazis and only recovered in Argentina last year must now be returned to the heir of its rightful owner, a court has
body: A painting which was stolen by the Nazis and only recovered in Argentina last year must now be returned to the heir of its rightful owner, a court has ruled. The late-baroque Portrait of a Lady was lost for 80 years until it was spotted in photographs of a house for sale near Buenos Aires.The house belonged to Patricia Kadgien, the daughter of a Nazi fugitive who had fled there after the Second World War, and she has now agreed to return the painting in exchange for not being prosecuted for concealing it from the authorities.Portrait of a Lady was among over 1,000 artworks looted from the collection of Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker after the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands in 1940.His daughter-in-law and sole heir Marei von Saher intends for the painting to be exhibited on a temporary loan at the Holocaust Museum of Buenos Aires to spread awareness of the issue, Argentine newspaper Clarin reports.Von Saher has previously said her family "aims to bring back every single artwork robbed from Jacques' collection, and to restore his legacy".This painting was first recognised in August 2025 by the Dutch Algemeen Dagblad (AD) newspaper on an estate agent's website of a property in the coastal town of Mar del Plata.It was hanging above a green sofa in the living room of Patricia Kadgien, whose father Friedrich Kadgien had been a top adviser to Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler's deputy. Goring plundered thousands of works across Europe.

schema.headline: Argentine couple to return Nazi-looted painting to rightful owner

title: 'It's like layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
description: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBCFigure caption, Watch: Moment workers are rescued from Nepal tu
body: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBCFigure caption, Watch: Moment workers are rescued from Nepal tunnelByTessa WongAsia Digital ReporterA tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border."It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced.The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people."I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors."We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to use explosives to clear the way, something they would "normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," Dix said. He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.At the same time, they discovered it was still full of water. Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.Image source, Nepalese Prime Minister's OfficeImage caption, Rescuers found a substantial amount of water in the tunnel as they dug through itFinally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," Dix explained.In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay". Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.Rescuers heading to 'Goldilocks zone'Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood did not reach the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers."Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," Dix said. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time. "It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located. "We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."Image source, Nepalese Prime Minister's OfficeImage caption, Rescuers had to pull the survivors through a tiny passageway created at the top of the rubble in the tunnel

schema.headline: 'It's like layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel

title: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views
description: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DCThe problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic object
body: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DCThe problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint.It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect.What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at.Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of stasis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait.US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position.US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war.My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration.Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, LondonI do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict.On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran.But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations.That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks.Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to IranThe latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.What is the White House's exit strategy? Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

schema.headline: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views

title: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy murder case as jury deadlocks
description: "At this point, I'm going to declare that the jury is deadlocked and I'm going to declare a mistrial," Judge William Sullivan told the jury on Friday,
body: "At this point, I'm going to declare that the jury is deadlocked and I'm going to declare a mistrial," Judge William Sullivan told the jury on Friday, dismissing them after weeks of testimony, seven days mulling Clancy's fate and the panel signalling three times that they were deadlocked. The deadlock - known as a hung jury - does not mean prosecutors have proven their case, nor does it mean the defendant is not guilty.A hearing was scheduled for 29 September, in which prosecutors could outline their next steps in the case. Meanwhile, the 36-year-old former nurse will remain held on the same murder charges and continue to stay in the mental health facility in which she is currently housed. Prosecutors could decide from a host of options as to what happens next, including holding another trial or coming to a plea agreement with Clancy over the strangulation of her children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan - in their Massachusetts home.After killing the children, Clancy cut herself ​with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to take her own life, which left her paralysed.Clancy does not deny killing the children in 2023 but pleaded not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges, with her lawyers arguing she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and so should not be held criminally responsible. "There will be no decisions made today," Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said on Friday concerning what could happen next in the case. He said he would meet the rest of their legal team to decide whether they would pursue a new trial. "The facts are Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and the evidence suggested to us that she was in control of her actions when she committed those homicides," Cruz said.Outside the court on Friday, Reddington said he believed 11 of the 12 jurors would have delivered a verdict that favoured Clancy had it not been for the one holdout.But it remains unclear what position any member of the jury took or what occurred in the deliberation room. For weeks, the case gripped the country and sparked debate over the topic of postpartum psychosis. Many followed along with livestreams of the trial, as family members and experts testified. Each day, more than 200 members of the media crowded the court and groups of supporters in varying sizes often gathered outside. The widespread attention even spurred comments on Friday from US President Donald Trump, who called the case a "horrible tragedy". "She did a horrible, horrible thing. Can't be worse," he said. "I assume there's going to be another trial." Trump added: "But you'll find out what the price to pay is. There'll be a price."If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external. www.befrienders.org.A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy murder case as jury deadlocks

title: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims
description: More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Br
body: More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.However in a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.When asked about if the prime minister believed the UK had the necessary forces to defend the sovereignty of the islands the spokesperson said "they will remain so far as long as the islanders wish"."Our armed forces are on standby 24/7 to protect the UK and our interests", the spokesperson added.Announcing his plan for sanctions in a national address on Thursday, Milei reiterated that the Falkland Islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.He said: "There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory."The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid."Milei described the Sea Lion oilfield as a "clear and present danger", and said if Argentina does not act swiftly, "they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before."He continued: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government." The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.  The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas."That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders." Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable"."Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands. "We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies". "If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others." Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

schema.headline: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims

title: Germany's far-right AfD bids for first taste of power in eastern vote
description: Germany is holding its breath this weekend as there is a seismic election in the country's east.The Alternative für Deutschland party is aiming to sec
body: Germany is holding its breath this weekend as there is a seismic election in the country's east.The Alternative für Deutschland party is aiming to secure a majority in the regional parliament of Saxony-Anhalt.An outright win would mark the first time a far-right party has held state-level power in the nation's post-war era.For the AfD's opponents, this is a point of serious peril. But the party sees it as a stepping stone towards its dreams of nationwide power.This is an election that could change German history.The result could also spell fresh trouble for embattled conservative (CDU) Chancellor Friedrich Merz, as rumours persist about whether he can see out his term in office.Booed during recent public appearances, Merz is hardly seen as an electoral asset.Perhaps the chancellor regrets a pledge to halt the rise of the far right, given that the exact opposite has happened.By contrast, the charismatic AfD lead candidate in the state - Ulrich Siegmund - appears to have enjoyed dominating discussion and media coverage.Dubbed "Germany's Most Dangerous Man" by Der Spiegel magazine, he has brushed off reports that people previously in the neo-Nazi scene are among those to hold influential roles around him.The 35-year-old can often be seen, including in his own many social media posts, amongst adoring crowds or happily riding a retro East German scooter.A lingering nostalgia for the past, alongside an acute dissatisfaction with the present, has fed the party's popularity in its eastern strongholds.Voters voice frustration with immigration, public safety, Germany's struggling economy, high energy costs and aid being sent abroad to countries like Ukraine.The party wants to segregate child refugees into special classes: "The refugee children should be given the message that their stay in Germany is only temporary."The manifesto claims that "sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles" have been aggressively promoted over "normal family" structures.LGBT rainbow flags should be banned from being flown at schools, the party argues, while children should be taught less about the Nazis and more about positive aspects of German history.On immigration, a task-force would be set up as part of plans to detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, while the party also calls for an end to "illegal, culturally alien" mass migration.The AfD's pro-Russia sympathies have also sparked claims that it cannot be trusted with sensitive intelligence. When a Russian army mug was spotted in the office of leading AfD figure Hans-Thomas Tillschneider in Saxony-Anhalt, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".That was as Berlin, this week, publicly blamed Moscow for a failed drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. The Kremlin has denied involvement.Meanwhile, German security sources have warned that Russian-backed disinformation campaigns, often against AfD rivals, have been escalating - something Moscow's representatives describe as "anti-Russian hysteria". State-level governments hold significant powers over areas including local education, policing and culture, while their delegates sit in the federal government's second chamber – the Bundesrat.An AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt would be able to implement changes locally and gain a louder voice on the national stage.The party remains strongest in the former communist east Germany but it is also leading the polls nationwide.That is despite warnings that it has morphed from a Eurosceptic party, founded in 2013, into one that flirts with, or attracts, extremist support.At one AfD rally, we saw a man wearing a T-shirt that read Arisch - the German word for Aryan that the Nazis used to promote their false theories of a master race.We do not know whether the man was a party supporter, a member or merely an attendee. He would not talk to us.Saxony-Anhalt is one of several states where the party is officially classed as right-wing extremist.Domestic intelligence charges the local branch with being infused by a "racist ideology" and anti-constitutional aims.The AfD, which says it is a conservative, libertarian movement, dismisses these designations as politicised smears and rejects any comparisons with National Socialism. Ulrich Siegmund has not ruled out getting rid of domestic intelligence (BfV) in the state if the AfD wins a majority.Other parties won't go into coalition with the AfD, as part of what is known as the Brandmauer or firewall that keeps the far right from government.That is why it must seek a parliamentary majority in order to be sure of securing power.In Saxony-Anhalt, it is no longer about creating cracks in the firewall but rather trying to bypass it altogether.Pulling that off will likely depend on whether other, smaller parties get enough votes in order to pass a 5% threshold that allows them to enter parliament.Politics is maths and Germany is no different, even if the maths can be quite convoluted.But if the AfD does score a decisive victory, then a party that uses anti-establishment rhetoric to grow its support will face a test it has never faced before.Grievances could still be laid at the door of the federal government in Berlin, but the AfD would no longer solely be able to rail against those in office because it would be in office itself.Saxony-Anhalt may be a relatively small state, by population, but it is about to host one hell of an election.

schema.headline: Germany's far-right AfD bids for first taste of power in eastern vote

title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in EuropeBySarah R
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in EuropeBySarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentAs summer temperatures in Europe smashed records and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.Poland's interior minister is clear."There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard.August campaign across Europe4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered.10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a warehouse of defence firm EMCO in Tryavna. In a statement, the company recalled previous blasts at its facilities which were investigated for links to Russia. "Human error is excluded," it said.13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion. The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons".15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested.Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators.25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe.30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires. One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out". An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities".The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz.Separately, police say they are hunting a climate extremist suspected of sabotage attacks this week on power substations in western Germany.Image source, EPAImage caption, The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firmsWhy is this happening now?Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store.The novelty now is the concentration of cases."The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says.She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine."We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something."Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes. After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid.There are other theories.To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses."Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank.He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe."They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it."The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia.2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland. One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger.Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport"That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds.It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit.But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible.Who are the suspected saboteurs?Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job.That would be unusual.The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs".They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction.In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers.The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online.The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable.The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted.So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success.In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned.Nato faced with Soviet-style campaignRussia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way.The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war."I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next."As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered.Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident.What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane?"I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

schema.headline: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect

title: Uganda's King Oyo death: Body of world's youngest traditional monarch returns amid succession row
description: Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja described him as a "symbol of unity" and praised his work raising awareness about HIV and Aids among young people.Oppo
body: Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja described him as a "symbol of unity" and praised his work raising awareness about HIV and Aids among young people.Opposition MPs also paid tribute, with acting opposition leader Patrick Nsamba Oshabe saying: "Heritage and development were never rivals in his hands."President Museveni has ordered an official burial for the monarch and national flags will fly at half-mast for three days around the funeral.On Wednesday, the Tooro kingdom's Prime Minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, said the king had asked officials not to disclose the seriousness of his illness because he believed he would recover and return to his people.He said the monarch had hoped to return home for this year's Empango - the annual celebration of his coronation - on 12 September."He was confident in his recovery," Akiiki said. His death has triggered uncertainty over the future of the monarchy as Oyo was not officially married.But Akiiki has said the king had a young son, whose identity would be revealed later in accordance with Tooro customs.President Museveni also said the king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, had told him that her son had left an heir.But Charles Kamurasi, who is head of the Babiito royal clan from which Tooro's kings are chosen, said he knew nothing about the reported child, prompting an unusual public disagreement among senior figures in the kingdom.Others within the royal clan have questioned why they were apparently unaware of the child."The prime minister is not supposed to talk about the king's heir. It is a cultural process," one royal clan member was quoted as saying by Uganda's state-owned New Vision newspaper."How can we, blood relatives, not know of the child, and the prime minister says he knows? That is totally out of order," the clan member added. Akiiki has since appealed for the dispute to be dealt with privately, saying he wanted to meet other elders to resolve their differences."Words spoken in moments of grief can deepen divisions that may take years to repair," he warned.The Ugandan government has also intervened, urging people not to spread speculation about the succession on social media.Culture Minister Henry Tumukunde said Ugandans should rely on official information from the government and the Tooro Kingdom, adding that any dispute would be dealt with under law governing traditional and cultural leaders."The whole world is watching how Uganda mourns its king," he said, urging people to show "restraint and respect".The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.King Oyo ascended the throne in 1995 and became an international curiosity because of his young age.Before his burial, a church funeral service will be held at a local church.His body will then be carried in a traditional procession to the Karambi Royal Tombs, with burial is expected to be completed by 14:00 local time.According to Tooro tradition, kings are not buried in the evening.

schema.headline: Uganda's King Oyo death: Body of world's youngest traditional monarch returns amid succession row

title: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
description: Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined. These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see coordinated
body: Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined. These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see coordinated vandalism. Yet here four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording".These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California, and Georgia.Proponents say they have made communities safer, and helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have led some to worry. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.Listen: ‘Big Surveillance’, Flock and ICEFounded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.But little is known about the extent that Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide, and estimates there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.For example, Houston's METRO Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show METRO has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year on year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship. And that's very problematic".There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.CCTV cameras, licence plate readers, and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice, and tune in to the capabilities of the technology around them.With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that doesn't mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI. The tool includes a database of over 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a License Agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. The office did not respond to requests for comment.Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime."It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer." Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had got lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable."But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching a licence plate.Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card."It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.In response, she's changed her commute to work: "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle, and Austin, Texas. In total, over 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in the month of August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice, external. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy. Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits, and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to 7 days, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.Flock Safety's CEO and founder, Garrett Langley, told the BBC it's up to individual cities to decide how long to store data, and what information to share with whom."I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says."As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find over 10,000 missing people. "The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."

schema.headline: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?

title: Niger coup attempt: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
description: When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it ha
body: When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny"."This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves."It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport."We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service."Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing."Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state."The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment."Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said."If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums."Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps."The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng."Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment."[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall."There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa."It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said."It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency."These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said."I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

schema.headline: Niger coup attempt: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?

title: Kenya's milk shortage: Chai lovers unhappy as cows run dry
description: Kenya's chai lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts o
body: Kenya's chai lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, is sometimes flavoured with ginger and spicesByBasillioh RukangaReporting fromNairobiKenyans love their milky tea, or chai, but some are facing the worrying possibility of doing without as the country has been hit by a milk shortage.A breakfast here is often incomplete without a cup of chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices. It is often served at meetings and during social visits, with many people taking the hot brew several times a day.But now some may have to do without as supermarket chilled sections are nearly empty. Retailers have upped the price and are limiting how much shoppers can take home.The government has put the dearth of milk in recent months down to drought, which has significantly reduced pasture and hampered production.But the recent shortages are unusual, with the country's industry regulator itself admitting to "supply constraints" and "low stock levels" across the country.Muthoni Macharia, who runs a restaurant in the capital, Nairobi, usually buys more than 70 packets of fresh milk - and is desperate and puzzled by the scarcity."Where has the milk gone?" she asked when the BBC spoke to her as she was out searching for at least a few packets to quench her customers thirst for chai.Image caption, For restaurant owner Muthoni Macharia, the milk shortage means a loss of businessMacharia says there have been shortages for about a week - and it was especially affecting her morning rush hour. Her regulars are not happy: some opting to take their tea black - but many will not."If they come in groups, and there's no milk tea, you see that's a loss for me," she said.Kenya is one of the leading milk producers on the continent.A long-established commercial dairy industry has led to pasteurised milk being very popular, particularly in urban areas, with Kenyans ranked among Africa's highest consumers, according to industry data.Raw and fermented milk is more widely drunk in rural areas.The milk shortage has sparked widespread public concern with some people promoting unfounded conspiracy theories about supermarkets deliberately trying to profit.According to the Kenya Dairy Board (KDB), the government body that oversees the dairy sector, formal milk deliveries to processors fell by 3.7% from 84.4 million litres in June to 81.3 million litres in July, while preliminary investigations suggest deliveries declined further in August.The Consumer Federation of Kenya (Cofek) says there has been a downward trend of supply since the beginning of the year.It attributes this to a delay in the seasonal rains, which has reduced the grazing ground available, coupled with a 45% rise in the cost of animal feed.Cofek has expressed concern over the rationing as well as the increasing cost, saying fresh milk prices have risen from 70 to 80 Kenyan shillings ($0.54 to $0.62; £0.40 to £0.46) a litre."This shortage was foreseeable, and in material part, avoidable," it says.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Normally fresh milk is in plentiful supply on supermarket shelves The consumer body says dairy processor New KCC, a state-owned company, and the KDB did not adequately absorb the milk surplus last year, adding that powder processed from the excess milk would have helped resolve the current crisis.Some of the milk processors in Kenya often reconvert the powder into the more-preferred liquid milk during dry seasons when the supply of fresh milk goes down."Had these buffers been in place, today's supply shock would have been substantially cushioned," Cofek says.It has demanded a recovery plan to include fodder and subsidy support for farmers.This would include waiving of taxes on animal feed inputs, as well as "active retail price monitoring to deter opportunity price gouging and rationing".In response to media enquiries, the dairy board's managing director William Maritim assured that despite the "temporary supply constraint", milk continued to be available.Fresh pasteurised milk, which has a shorter shelf life, had been more affected than the more long-life UHT milk, he said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dairy cows need to eat well to produce milkCustomers at Nairobi supermarkets on the hunt for milk told the BBC they were worried about rising costs."Sometimes when I go to the supermarket I find there is none. When I do find some, the price has gone up. Today it is this price, tomorrow it has gone up again," said Bernard Abok, who does his shopping after finishing work.Patricia Gathoni said if the prices kept going up she would have to rethink what she gave her children, saying she had resorted to adding water to the milk that she managed to buy.On Thursday, agriculture ministry officials held a meeting with the association of dairy processors about the problem, with the ministry committing to support farmers, stabilise milk supply and protect consumers.The ministry's top official in charge of livestock development, Jonathan Mueke, said the immediate focus was to get more feed for farmers, including through duty-free importation of yellow maize.He said they were also looking at longer-term solutions that would manage stability across periods when there was surplus milk and when there were shortages.Reports of milk going to waste are not uncommon during periods of a dairy glut. Farmers have often complained about how little they are paid for their perishable produce at such times - but they have few options because of limited processing or storage capacity.According to Mueke, the government is considering setting up a fund to help support the preservation of milk during such periods.In the meantime, the government is also considering temporarily importing milk from the neighbouring countries to ease the shortage.For the devoted Kenyan chai lover, that may offer some respite.Additional reporting by Ahmed BahajjYou may also be interested in:

schema.headline: Kenya's milk shortage: Chai lovers unhappy as cows run dry

title: Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem
description: Almost 100% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and it produces so much it earns nearly $200m (£147m) each year exporting hydroelectricity t
body: Almost 100% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and it produces so much it earns nearly $200m (£147m) each year exporting hydroelectricity to India and Bangladesh.But the very glaciers and mountains giving Nepal this massive natural advantage are succumbing to global warming - and last Wednesday's deadly floods have laid bare the risks to the nation's hydropower ambitions.More than 1,300 people were killed, while thousands more are still missing.The floods, which destroyed entire villages near the border of Nepal and Tibet, severely damaged 12 hydropower plants in the Trishuli River basin and knocked out more than 10% of Nepal's total power generation capacity. Operators tell the BBC they don't yet know if any of these facilities can be brought back to operation.The state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority, which owns six of the 12 damaged facilities, has assured Nepalese households that supply remains adequate. But its spokesman Rajan Dhakal acknowledges that with climate-related disasters becoming more frequent, "the time has come for a rethink of our hydropower policy".Only two-thirds of people in Nepal had access to electricity in 2010, and even connected households would face power cuts for up to 16 hours a day.An expansion of hydropower infrastructure alongside efforts to tackle corruption and boost energy imports from India to fill seasonal gaps meant that by 2018, most of Nepal was enjoying 24 hours of power supply per day.At present, there are 225 hydropower plants across Nepal with more than 3,900MW of installed capacity, according to the Nepal Electricity Authority - capable of powering some three million households simultaneously.Hundreds more such facilities are either being constructed or in the pipeline. Most of them are built high up in the mountains, where they can seize fast-flowing currents to generate power. These projects require little to no storage system.However, with the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas warming 50% faster than the global average, they face greater environmental risks. Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier and its bedrock as the cause of last week's flash flood.While scientists say it is too soon to draw any firm links to climate change, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority previously said more than nine in 10 disaster events recorded between 2018 and 2024 were "related to climate".Nepal's former Energy Minister Kulman Ghising, who called the catastrophic deluge a "once-in-a-century" event, says it holds lessons for designing plants and picking sites where they are built."We need to design the plants [to be more] resilient to the floods and, most importantly, adopt early-warning systems as well as robust emergency evacuation measures," he told environmental news outlet Mongabay.Potentially hundreds of hydropower labourers, engineers and residents are thought to be trapped inside the mud-filled tunnels of these plants since the floods hit.A "rethink" of Nepal's hydropower strategy could involve reservoir-based plants that need not be situated up in the mountains, says Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority. These could allow water to be stored and released as needed, but would also involve significant economic and environmental costs.Some question if Nepal has been too reliant on hydropower."We should not be putting all our eggs in one basket in these dangerous times," says renewable energy expert Kushal Gurung, who founded the clean tech firm WindPower Nepal."We need to seriously embrace other alternatives as well, like solar and wind. And for that we will need to revise our energy policy that is at the moment very pro-hydropower," he says.The claim is echoed by Vivek Shastry, researcher at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who argues that "meaningful additions of wind and solar generation is a resilience strategy that can limit single-point or interconnected electricity system failures in the future".A report from the German aid agency suggests the technical potential for energy production from solar power in Nepal is around 10 times larger, external than that of hydropower.  Puspa Sharma, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore's Institute of South Asian Studies, agrees Nepal has to diversify its energy sources, but warns this can be done "only to a limited extent"."While there is untapped capacity in wind and solar, hydropower really is the one that gives Nepal massive competitive advantage vis-a-vis its South Asian neighbours," he says, citing various studies comparing renewable energy potential in the region.Hydropower continues to dominate large-scale investments in Nepal, and some climate activists say the funding has continued despite known disaster risks.The Upper Trishuli-1 project, which has been all but destroyed after last week's floods, was one of Nepal's largest foreign direct investment ventures, valued at about $647m. Its backers include the Asian Development Bank and the International Finance Corporation.The Upper Trishuli 3A, which has also been severely hit, was funded by China's Export-Import Bank.Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People, says international lenders were "acutely aware of the extreme danger to which they were exposing thousands of labourers, officials, residents, rivers, infrastructure and landscape"."Their own reports repeatedly highlighted it. But they did not take any preventive steps, did not demand stringent checks and balances, nor were they prepared for a calamity they knew could occur," he says.History has already shown the Trishuli River basin to be volatile, Thakkar says, pointing to how it had been hit by floods in the last two years. In September 2024, an unprecedented cloudburst over the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river basins sparked flash floods in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading - settlements by the river that are also among the hardest hit from last week's floods.Then in July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet's Gyirong county burst and swept down this very same stretch of river into Nepal, killing at least 11 people. That flood damaged critical infrastructure and halted trade along the busy Nepal-China corridor. The border crossing was shut for nearly six months and had only reopened on 1 January this year.Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority admits that even if climate risk assessments were carried out correctly, "the designing of the plants may not have been done accordingly"."Clearly we will need to improve in the way we build and operate our hydropower plants," he adds.Private operators are already feeling the financial impact. Insurers have paid out around $40m for flood-related damage to more than 20 privately owned plants over the past three years, according to Uttam Bhlon Lama from the Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal.He warns insurance premiums are rising significantly and making the cost of doing business "unfeasible".

schema.headline: Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem

title: 'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC
description: Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who were shot dead this week when settlers and soldiers entered a Palestinian village in the o
body: Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who were shot dead this week when settlers and soldiers entered a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank.The killing of Omar al-Naasan and Khalil Abu Alia comes amid near-daily attacks by Jewish settlers in the village of al-Mughayyir, south of Nablus."We expect that when our sons walk in the street, they are likely to return to you injured or killed," Mohammed Al-Naasan, Omar's father, told the BBC.Israel's military says it fired on "instigators of a violent riot" and that the incident is under review.The United Nations says more than 80 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the territory since the beginning of the year.More on this story: Palestinian teens killed during settler attack on West Bank village

schema.headline: 'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC

title: Russian drone hits Ukranian security headquarters, Zelensky says
description: "All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram."I instruc
body: "All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram."I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response."Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building.Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses"."Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added.Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices.A nearby café was damaged and one customer was taken to hospital after the strike.Stanislav Zavertaylo, co-owner of the popular Zavertailo chain, told the BBC that this was his third café to have been damaged since the start of the full-scale invasion."Now I'm in shock because there's a lot of damage. All the windows are broken, there's a lot of glass, garbage" he added.The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa.In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets.In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack.

schema.headline: Russian drone hits Ukranian security headquarters, Zelensky says

title: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
description: The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.The distortio
body: The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.The distortion of his map is a result of the fact that it is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.Whenever a map of the world is drawn, compromises need to be made. The Mercator map accomodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing larger.In an effort to address this, a team of cartographers in 2018 created an equal area map they called the Equal Earth projection.In February, the AU's 54 member states adopted it, and said it "more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa".Online campaign group #CorrectTheMap said: "You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare."Ahead of Friday's vote, Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told news agency Reuters: "A fair world begins with a fair map."He told a UN briefing earlier: "A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood."He had the backing of the French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, who said his ministry was going to stop using the Mercator map, external."Changing the map obviously doesn't change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," he said.But Yaryna Ferencevych, a US representative at the UN, said the resolution mocked the work and purpose of the UN General Assembly, external."Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th Century, and their role in promoting reparations and 'cognitive justice'," she said.In March, the US was also critical when a resolution was adopted declaring the transatlantic slave trade "the gravest crime against humanity".

schema.headline: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
